name: New Kingdom Egypt
title: Social Hierarchy of Ancient Egypt: From Pharaoh to Enslaved

tiers.name: The pharaoh
tiers.you: You are hailed as the “good god”: in theory you own all the land and command the army, and you alone stand between Egypt and its gods.
tiers.kid: The pharaoh was Egypt’s ruler, who led the army, made the laws and was honoured almost like a god.
tiers.rise: Kingship passed by birth, usually to the king’s son, but when a dynasty failed the throne could go to the men who served it: Ay and the general Horemheb rose from the royal court, and Horemheb’s vizier became king as Ramesses I in 1292 BCE.
tiers.why: The king stood apart from all other Egyptians.

tiers.name: High officials
tiers.you: You serve the king in high office, overseeing his granaries, his building works or a conquered province, and you are preparing a painted tomb in the Theban hills; all of it depends on the pharaoh’s favour.
tiers.kid: Officials such as the vizier ran Egypt for the pharaoh, keeping its records and judging its court cases.
tiers.rise: Most officials were the sons of officials and had trained as scribes, but the king could raise a capable outsider, such as Bay, a commoner of West Asian origin who became chancellor and the power behind the throne at the end of the 19th Dynasty.
tiers.why: Below the king stood the small circle of officials who ran his government, the elite that Egyptian texts called the pat.

tiers.name: Priests
tiers.you: You serve the god in shifts, shaving your head and body and washing several times a day before you enter the temple; when your turn of duty ends, you go back to your own work.
tiers.kid: Priests looked after the temples, where they washed and dressed the gods’ statues and gave them food every day.
tiers.rise: The king appointed the high priests, often as a reward for a favoured official, while lesser posts passed from father to son or were filled by the priests themselves; at the end of the period the army officer Herihor became High Priest of Amun and ruled Upper Egypt (about 1080 BCE).
tiers.why: Priests served the gods in the king’s place.

tiers.name: Scribes
tiers.you: You sit with your palette and papyrus, counting grain, cattle and fields for the tax records, and your writing spares you the corvée that farmers owe.
tiers.kid: Scribes kept Egypt’s records, writing down harvests, taxes and court cases on rolls of papyrus.
tiers.rise: Boys, mostly the sons of scribes, learned the craft at school or from their fathers; a gifted scribe could rise into the high offices of state, which were closed to men who could not write.
tiers.why: Scribes kept the records on which the state ran.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You march with the pharaoh’s army to Nubia or the Levant for regular pay; if you fight bravely the king may reward you with gold and captives, and as a veteran you may be granted a plot of land.
tiers.kid: Egyptian soldiers fought on foot or from fast, two-wheeled chariots pulled by horses.
tiers.rise: War was the quickest way up for an able man: soldiers won rewards and land, and Horemheb, a general under Tutankhamun, became king himself.
tiers.why: The New Kingdom was born in the war against the Hyksos, and its pharaohs turned the old levies into a standing professional army.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.term: hemu (craftsmen), sedjem-ash (servants in the Place of Truth)
tiers.you: You cut and paint the pharaoh’s tomb eight days out of ten and are paid in grain from the state’s stores; when the rations fail to come, you and your crew lay down your tools.
tiers.kid: Skilled craftsmen built and painted the royal tombs, and they went on strike when their food did not arrive.
tiers.rise: Places in the royal crew were prized and usually passed from father to son; the village was abandoned under Ramesses XI, when tomb robbery, Libyan raids and civil war brought the work to an end.
tiers.why: Craftsmen ranked above farmers, but most worked for the state or the temples, in workshops attached to the temples and palaces, and were paid in rations from their stores.

tiers.name: Farmers
tiers.you: You plough and sow as the Nile flood falls, hand a share of your harvest to the temple or the king, and can be called away to dig canals or work in the quarries.
tiers.kid: Most Egyptians were farmers who grew wheat, barley and flax in fields watered by the Nile’s yearly flood.
tiers.rise: A farmer’s son could enlist in the army and earn rewards or a plot of land; a low flood or a debt could push a family into tenancy or servitude.
tiers.why: Most Egyptians were farmers living in mud-brick villages along the Nile.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken in war and handed by the king to a temple or an official; you brew, weave or work the fields for your owner, who can sell you or hire you out.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many were prisoners taken in war.
tiers.rise: Freedom could come through marriage to a free person or dedication to a temple’s service, and an enslaved woman who bore children for a childless couple could win her freedom; some captives were made soldiers.
tiers.why: The wars of the New Kingdom made it Egypt’s great age of foreign slavery.
